new_statements.quote: Aquest argument, que ha estat aplicat a la Romània deçà la Mediterrània, quadra molt bé amb el que sabem de l’accent en amazic, on no hi ha síl·labes de tonicitat veritablement predominant [n. 3213: Val a dir que, en el conjunt de Tamazga actual, hi ha casos que ens obligarien a matisar aquesta afirmació (cf. VYCICHL 1984); en general, però, des del punt de vista fonològic, l’accent d’intensitat no permet establir distincions fonològiques i, des del punt de vista fonètic, fins i tot si en alguns contextos es pot observar una certa preeminència en la tonicitat d’alguna síl·laba, en cap cas té una intensitat comparable a la que té, posem per cas, en les llengües romàniques.]
new_statements.translation: This argument [that a strong intensity accent favoured keeping quality distinctions in stressed vowels elsewhere in the Romance area], which has been applied to the Romània on this side of the Mediterranean, squares very well with what we know of the accent in Amazigh, where there are no syllables of truly predominant stress [n. 3213: Admittedly, across present-day Tamazgha there are cases that would oblige us to qualify this statement (cf. Vycichl 1984); in general, however, from the phonological point of view the intensity accent does not serve to establish phonological distinctions and, from the phonetic point of view, even if in some contexts a certain pre-eminence in the stress of some syllable can be observed, in no case does it have an intensity comparable to the one it has, say, in the Romance languages.]

new_statements.rule_in_words: Author asserts that Amazigh (Berber) has no syllable with truly predominant stress and that intensity accent is not phonologically distinctive, and uses this (together with the 3-vowel paleo-Amazigh system) to explain vowel confusions in African Latin inscriptions; by implication the ancient substrate language (paleo-Amazigh = Numidian) is taken to have lacked a strong/contrastive word stress. No positional rule is given.
new_statements.exceptions: n. 3213: 'hi ha casos [in present-day Tamazgha] que ens obligarien a matisar aquesta afirmació (cf. Vycichl 1984)' -- i.e. some modern Berber varieties do show accentual phenomena.
new_statements.identity_note: Glottolog files this thesis under Numidian [nxm] and it is the live Glottolog's most extensive description. Its object, 'paleoamazic', is the ancient Amazigh (Berber) language of all North Africa as reflected in Greek/Latin sources and Libyco-Berber epigraphy, i.e. the languoid Glottolog calls Numidian plus ancient onomastics from Egypt to Tingitana. The accent sentence quoted below, however, is phrased about 'amazic' (Amazigh/Berber in general, present tense, citing Vycichl 1984 on modern varieties) and is used as a substrate/adstrate argument for African Latin; it is an inference projected onto the ancient language, not an observation of Numidian prosody (which the consonantal script cannot record).
